title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) loop affects verifier-detected safety violations for LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 intent→configuration tasks stratified into VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change clusters) we compared: (1) baseline — a single LLM proposal produced once per task, and (2) guarded — the identical shared LLM proposal validated by a deterministic netops verifier and subjected to up to one automated repair iteration if the verifier flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002; paired-bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). The preregistered exact McNemar two-sided test was implemented as an exact binomial on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01); with n = 1 and n10 = 1 the archived two-sided p = 1.00 under that convention. Interpretation: on this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and the selected model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; the measured marginal verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric is therefore small, though the verifier corrected one concrete baseline failure. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being applied to NetOps tasks such as translation of operator intent to device configuration, multi-step change planning, and configuration repair. System reports and surveys emphasize that operational safety depends heavily on surrounding engineering: deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback mechanisms [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. A widely proposed operational pattern is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): an LLM generates a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks a set of formalized properties, and automated or human-in-the-loop repairs are applied for violations. Despite conceptual consensus, controlled measurements that isolate the marginal contribution of a verifier (holding the model’s proposal fixed) are scarce. Practitioners therefore lack quantified guidance on whether modest verifier+repair budgets materially reduce verifier-detected safety violations when baseline LLM proposals are already high-quality.

We address this precise operational question with a preregistered paired experiment that isolates verifier+repair impact under canonical, deterministic semantics. Our objective is deliberately narrow: given identical initial proposals (shared_initial_candidate semantics), how much does integrating a deterministic verifier and at most one automated repair iteration reduce verifier-detected safety violations compared to the same LLM alone? The preregistered design, deterministic task generator, archived prompts, verifier traces, and analysis artifacts are included in the evidence bundle to permit deterministic audit.
sections.related_work:
Deterministic and formal network-configuration verification tools (header-space analysis, route-model verifiers, Batfish-style analyzers) provide machine-checkable properties such as reachability, isolation, and update atomicity; these methods underpin verifier-in-the-loop system designs [Beckett et al., 2017]. Recent NetOps/AIOps and intent-translation literature documents LLM-based configuration generation and agentic NetOps frameworks while advocating guardrails for operational reliability (e.g., INTA, Confucius, and other agentic NetOps proposals) [INTA, 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–verify–repair patterns appear across structured-generation domains and have been proposed to reduce incorrect or unsafe outputs [PoeTone; INTA].

Separate bodies of work catalog LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, tool-integration errors) and recommend verification or human oversight as mitigations [Owen, 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2025]. What is less prevalent in the supplied evidence is a controlled, preregistered ablation that quantifies the marginal verifier effect while keeping the LLM’s initial output identical for both arms. This study contributes such an artifact-backed measurement and situates it relative to prior system and verification work.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. We preregistered study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026, freezing research questions, inclusion/exclusion rules, deterministic task seeds, estimands, analysis executor, multiplicity plan, retry policy, and stopping rule before observing outcomes. The primary confirmatory hypothesis tested whether an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration reduces verifier-detected safety violations relative to an LLM-only single proposal (paired within-task). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations. The preregistration and artifacts are archived (preregistration SHA-256 recorded in the execution manifest).

Task generation and strata. A deterministic synthetic corpus of 500 intent→configuration tasks was generated with deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 using preregistered seeds. Tasks were stratified into three clusters per the preregistration: VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change. The realized confirmatory set contained 500 complete pairs and matched the preregistered stratification allocation (per-cluster planned allocation: VLAN-change = 167, ACL-change = 167, static-route-change = 166); no confirmatory exclusions occurred. The generator constrained allowed fields to {admin, mtu, vlan} to match the deterministic verifier’s modeled coverage; the complete task manifest (inputs, seeds, expected_final_state, required_sequence) is archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl and the deterministic_reconciliation artifact verifies task_count = 500.

Generation semantics and experimental control. To isolate verifier marginal effect we used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (independent_condition_generation = false). For each task the pipeline produced a single shared LLM proposal that served as the baseline output and was validated by the guarded arm. The guarded path invoked the automated single-repair call only if the verifier reported a preregistered high/medium-severity violation on that shared candidate. This semantics prevents conflation with verifier-guided regeneration and isolates the pure effect of verification plus at most one repair applied to the same initial proposal.

Models, adapter, and verifier. Requested LLM = gpt-5-mini called via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter (provider logged as openai_responses); model parameters are archived in execution/model_configuration.json. The deterministic verifier used for gating and scoring was deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the validator specification and the mapping of violation codes to severity are archived. The guarded arm permitted at most one automated repair iteration per the preregistration.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes. The run completed with complete_pair_count = 500 and model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair-stage calls = 1). Aggregated per-condition counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). The paired contingency table (guarded × baseline; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002.

Exact McNemar two-sided p-value and CI. The archived confirmatory test uses an exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention: for observed discordant counts n = n10 + n01 the test performs an exact binomial test on n10 with p = 0.5 and returns a two-sided p via p_two-sided = 2 × min{P(X ≤ n10), P(X ≥ n10)} for X ∼ Binomial(n, 0.5), truncated at 1.0. For the observed discordant counts (n = 1, n10 = 1) this produces two-sided p = 1.00 under the archived convention; the archive records this implementation choice and the computed p (analysis/results.json and analysis_log.jsonl). The paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute difference is [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729), computed with paired resampling preserving pair units; bootstrap parameters and code are archived.

Repair activity and the single corrected episode. Observed repair-stage provider calls = 1; that single repair produced the sole discordant outcome (n10 = 1): the guarded arm converted one baseline-detected violation into a verified pass. The run-level manifests and reconciliation artifacts confirm exactly one such episode exists (deterministic_reconciliation.json and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The precise pair/episode identifier and the full validator diagnostics and repair-stage traces for that episode are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl and its associated provider-call traces (execution/provider_calls/*). To preserve deterministic auditability without reprinting large raw traces in the manuscript, readers may locate the episode by filtering the archived execution/raw_results.jsonl for entries where the baseline scoring indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) and guarded scoring indicates pass == 1; that filter deterministically returns the single discordant episode and its archived validator_trace and repair_provider_trace. The archived record shows that the verifier flagged a preregistered severity violation on the shared initial candidate and that a single automated repair call produced a final configuration that passed the verifier; full per-field validator diagnostics and repair texts are available in the evidence bundle.

Power and ceiling effects. The preregistration targeted power to detect an absolute 10-percentage-point reduction assuming baseline error prevalence ≈ 0.30 (N ≈ 384). Observed baseline failure prevalence was one in 500, producing a ceiling effect that reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute improvements. Consequently the single discordant outcome limits inferential power on the primary paired test despite the preregistered analysis plan. All diagnostics (missingness_summary.csv, contamination_summary.csv, deterministic_reconciliation.json) indicate no confirmatory exclusions or failed episodes.
sections.discussion:
Operational interpretation. Under the constrained experimental regime—single requested LLM (gpt-5-mini), shared_initial_candidate semantics, a deterministic verifier modeling a limited feature set (allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}), and up to one automated repair iteration—the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals and the marginal measured pass-rate benefit of adding the verifier was small (0.002). This conditional result illustrates a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal quality is very high for verifier-modeled properties, a modest verifier+repair budget may yield negligible measurable gains on a composite pass/fail metric even though the verifier can correct rare concrete failures (as observed).

Design-choice implications. The shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolate the verifier+repair effect conditional on identical proposals. This operational posture is relevant when deployments constrain model-call budgets or require that a single human-reviewed proposal be repaired rather than regenerated. Alternative operational choices—verifier-guided regeneration, multiple repair iterations, or cost-weighted objectives—may produce larger effect sizes and merit separate preregistered evaluation.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is supported by preregistration, deterministic task seeds, and automated replacement rules; no manual adjudication occurred. Construct validity is limited by the verifier’s modeled property set: success==no high/medium-severity violations is defined relative to the archived validator coverage and severity mapping; properties outside that scope are not measured. External validity is limited by single-model testing, synthetic tasks, and constrained feature scope; results do not imply cross-vendor or production generality.

Statistical nuance. The archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the chosen exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the empirical discordant counts (n = 1). Small-sample exact p-values here reflect limited discordant data rather than evidence of equivalence. The paired-bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.006] provides complementary uncertainty quantification for the absolute difference.
sections.conclusion: We performed a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) that isolated the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The LLM produced near-ceiling verifier-scoped proposals (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), giving an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the run’s exact-binomial convention). The measurement illustrates a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal quality is very high for verifier-modeled properties and the verifier’s coverage is limited, the measurable marginal pass-rate benefit of a modest verifier+repair budget can be negligible on a composite pass/fail metric, although the verifier can correct rare concrete failures. Practitioners should (1) measure baseline proposal error prevalence before allocating repair budgets; (2) align verifier coverage with operator-critical properties; and (3) choose generation semantics (shared candidate vs regeneration) to match operational priorities. The full preregistration, code, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection of every claim made here.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; task payloads constrained to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single requested model family (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — no claim of multi-model or cross-validator generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the small discordant count.

The single discordant episode (the sole task where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl in the evidence bundle. To inspect it deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair entries where the baseline scoring outcome indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while the guarded scoring outcome indicates pass == 1; because only one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, this lookup returns the single episode and its provider-call traces. The validator violation-code→severity mapping is archived in the execution manifest and validator-spec artifacts in the bundle.
